I've fixed it: two rules with the same path now only count as duplicates if they share a method. Before this, `Map([Rule("/", methods=["GET"]), Rule("/", methods=["POST"])])` raised `DuplicateRuleError`, which breaks a very common setup. `tests/test_routing.py` passes (153 tests), and the full suite passed (972 tests) before I added the last test and some docstrings.

**The fix**
- **`src/werkzeug/routing/rules.py`:** I added a private `Rule._is_duplicate(other)`. It is true only when `self == other` and the methods overlap. `None` on either side overlaps everything. As the issue suggested, `__eq__` is unchanged; `provides_defaults_for` relies on it with `self != rule`, so loosening it would have changed that behaviour.
- **`src/werkzeug/routing/matcher.py`:** `StateMachineMatcher.add` now calls `rule._is_duplicate(existing)` instead of `rule == existing`.

**`strict_slashes` and `merge_slashes`**
Both were already handled, because the comparison works on the parsed path parts (`_parts`):
- **`merge_slashes`:** slashes are merged before the path is parsed. So with it on, `/a//b` and `/a/b` are duplicates (they match the same URLs). With it off, they are separate rules.
- **`strict_slashes`:** this only controls redirects. Two copies of `/a/` are duplicates whatever their setting. `/a` and `/a/` are different parts, so they are never compared.

**Tests and docs**
- **Tests:** I added tests for:
  - methods that don't overlap
  - methods that do overlap, including `None` against a list and `["GET"]` against `["HEAD"]` (`GET` adds `HEAD` automatically)
  - `merge_slashes` both on and off
  - `strict_slashes` not mattering
  - a leaf and a branch with the same path
- **Docs:** I updated the duplicate-rule paragraph in `docs/routing.rst` to cover methods and both slash options.

**Why `Rule.methods` can be `None`**
`None` means the rule accepts any method. It is not "defaults to GET", which is why there's no GET logic anywhere. The `Rule` docstring says "If not specified, all methods are allowed", and the code follows that:
- **Matching:** a `None` rule never raises `MethodNotAllowed`.
- **URL building:** `suitable_for` skips the method check.
- **Duplicates:** the new check treats `None` as overlapping every other rule.

`None` is different from any set you could write out, because it also accepts methods nobody has thought of. I left it alone, since changing it would break existing code.

Nothing is committed.
